summary: A 1975 proposal for changes to the protocol between hosts and IMPs, including addressing hosts on more than 63 IMPs and other backward compatible expansions. It was replaced by RFC 704. See also RFC 690 and RFC 692.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 687 sketches changes to the ARPANET IMP/host protocol so it could address hosts on more IMPs. It proposes larger fields and a period when old and new message formats would both work.

questions: how did the imp host protocol change in 1975
how many imps could the arpanet address
subtitle: A 1975 design sketch for expanding the IMP/host protocol while retaining old formats.

tldr.problem: The ARPA Network was approaching the existing IMP/host addressing limit, with almost 60 IMPs already in service.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal expands the leader and address fields, adds message-length and handling information, and supports old and new formats in parallel.
tldr.outcome: This design note was updated by RFC 690 and obsoleted by RFC 704.

facts.label: Address field
facts.value: 24 bits: 16-bit IMP address and 8-bit host address

sections.title: Why Expand the Protocol
sections.content:
RFC 687 sketches an expansion of the protocol between an Interface Message Processor (IMP) and its host. The plan would allow hosts to be addressed on more than 63 IMPs, as the network was nearing that limit.

The note aims to correct existing limits without making fundamental changes to the protocol. It describes the expansion as backward compatible and assumes familiarity with Section 3 of BBN Report 1822.
sections.plainLanguage: The network was close to the protocol's limit on IMP addresses. This note proposes changes that add capacity without replacing the whole protocol.

sections.title: Changes to the Message Leader
sections.content:
The proposal expands the leader from two to five 16-bit words. The address field grows to 24 bits, divided into a 16-bit IMP address and an 8-bit host address. A new optional 13-bit field lets a source host give the message length in bits.

The handling-type field grows to 8 bits to allow different handling characteristics, including priority, non-priority, packet counts per message, unordered messages, and guaranteed capacity. Other proposed changes include moving unordered-message indication into the handling type, changing fake host addresses, and adding the host address to an IMP-to-host NOP.
sections.plainLanguage: The message leader gains larger address space and fields for message length and handling. The note also proposes changes to how some message types and host addresses are represented.

sections.title: Supporting Old and New Formats
sections.content:
IMPs would support the old and new formats in parallel during a gradual transition. A host would choose a format through its host-to-IMP NOP message and could switch formats for debugging.

A host using the old format could not address IMPs numbered above 63. Where possible, IMPs would convert between formats so old-format and new-format hosts could communicate. The note also proposes a non-blocking interface that would let an IMP refuse a message and later ask the host to resend it.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts could choose either format while IMPs handled both. The IMP would translate between formats where possible, but the old format could not name higher-numbered IMPs.
